sections.h: The Epistle of Barnabas: the way of light and the way of darkness
sections.b: Barnabas ends its "knowledge" of Scripture (1-17) and turns to "another knowledge and teaching": "There are two ways of teaching and of power, one of light and one of darkness" (Barnabas 18:1). Light-bringing angels of God stand over one, angels of Satan over the other. The way of light (19) is a list of commands, many word for word with Didache 1-4: love the one who made you, no sexual sin, no abortion, share everything, confess your sins. The way of "the Black One" (20) is "crooked and full of cursing," a list of sins and of the people who do them. Kirsopp Lake gives three views of how the two texts are related: Barnabas used the Didache, the Didache used Barnabas, or both used a common source, which "probably the majority of scholars" prefer, many thinking it a Jewish teaching for converts. The one Latin manuscript of Barnabas stops before the Two Ways (17:2).
sections.refs: Barnabas 18:1-2; Barnabas 19:1-12; Barnabas 20:1-2; Didache 1:1-5:2; Deuteronomy 30:15-19; Matthew 7:13-14

common: Barnabas 18-20 and Didache 1-5 share one Two Ways teaching, probably from a common source.
uncommon: The Jewish Encyclopedia thought the Two Ways was "probably attached" to Barnabas "by some copyist at a much later time"; the Latin version lacks it.

sections.h: The Epistle of Barnabas: figures everywhere
sections.b: Barnabas uses the word typos, "figure," more than any other early Christian writing of its size. The scapegoat is "a figure of Jesus" (Barnabas 7:7, 7:10), the wool among the thorns a figure for the church (7:11), the red heifer and its wool on wood a figure of the cross (8:1), Moses' outstretched arms and the bronze snake figures of the crucified (12:2, 12:5-6), and Jacob's crossed hands a figure of the people to come (13:5). Unlike Hebrews, which reads the rites as shadows that were really kept until Christ came (Hebrews 8:5; 10:1), Barnabas says they were never meant to be kept literally (9:4; 10:2). That makes his typology the edge case against which later Christian readers measured their own.
sections.refs: Barnabas 7:7-11; Barnabas 8:1; Barnabas 12:2-7; Barnabas 13:5; Hebrews 8:5; Hebrews 10:1; Romans 5:14

sections.h: The Epistle of Barnabas: allegory against the letter
sections.b: Barnabas promises "perfect knowledge" along with faith (Barnabas 1:5): the hidden meaning of the law. Pigs, birds of prey and scaleless fish stand for kinds of people (10:3-5); chewing the cud is thinking over the word (10:11); the 318 men Abraham circumcised spell Jesus and the cross in Greek numbers (9:8). Lake writes that the writer "carries a symbolical exegesis as far as did Philo; indeed he goes farther and apparently denies any literal significance at all to the commands of the Law." Philo, the Jewish teacher of Alexandria, also read the clean animals' signs as lessons of the soul (On the Special Laws 4.106-108), but kept the laws. Barnabas's claim that the literal sense came from "an evil angel" (9:4) is where allegory turns against the text itself.

sections.h: The Epistle of Barnabas: 318, and six thousand years
sections.b: Two number readings stand out in Barnabas. First, the 318 men of Abraham's household (Genesis 14:14, joined to Genesis 17:23-27): in Greek numerals, 18 is IH, the first letters of Jesus, and 300 is T, the shape of the cross (Barnabas 9:7-8). Clement of Alexandria repeats it (Stromata 6.11). Second, the days of creation: since "the Lord's day will be like a thousand years" (Psalm 90:4; 2 Peter 3:8), six days mean six thousand years of history, the seventh is the Son's rest, and an "eighth day" begins a new world (Barnabas 15:4-8).
sections.refs: Barnabas 9:7-8; Barnabas 15:4-9; Genesis 14:14; Genesis 17:23-27; Psalm 90:4; 2 Peter 3:8

sections.h: The Epistle of Barnabas: the world week
sections.b: Barnabas reads Genesis 2:2 with Psalm 90:4: "in six thousand years the Lord will bring everything to its end" (Barnabas 15:4). Then the Son will come, end "the time of the lawless one," judge the ungodly, change the sun, moon and stars, and "Then he will truly rest on the seventh day" (15:5). After it comes "an eighth day, which is the beginning of another world" (15:8). Barnabas does not say plainly whether the seventh day is a thousand-year reign on earth before the new world, as one reading of Revelation 20 holds, or the final rest itself. His remark that believers do not yet rule the earth but will (6:17-19) fits the first view, and Ladeuze (Catholic Encyclopedia) calls him "a millenarian."

sections.h: The Epistle of Barnabas: the fast and the two goats
sections.b: Barnabas reads the Day of Atonement as a prophecy of Jesus. The command to fast on pain of death (Leviticus 23:29), and priests alone eating the goat's entrails with vinegar, point to the vinegar and gall at the cross (Barnabas 7:3-5). The two goats, "fine ones and alike," are one Christ: the one offered is his death, and the cursed one, spat on, stabbed and wreathed with scarlet wool, is the one his crucifiers will recognize at his coming (7:6-10). Many of these details are not in Leviticus 16, but the Mishnah knows a crimson strip tied to the goat's horns and Babylonian Jews who plucked its hair (Mishnah Yoma 6:4-6), and "the Babylonians" who ate the atonement goat raw (Mishnah Menachot 11:7). Justin Martyr also reads the two goats as Christ's two appearances (Dialogue with Trypho 40).

sections.h: The Epistle of Barnabas: the heifer as Jesus
sections.b: Barnabas 8 reads Numbers 19 point by point. Men "whose sins are complete" offer the heifer; children gather the ashes, tie scarlet wool and hyssop to wood, and sprinkle the people (Barnabas 8:1). The heifer is Jesus, the men are those who led him to slaughter, the sprinkling children are the apostles, twelve for the tribes, and three for Abraham, Isaac and Jacob (8:2-4); the wool on wood is "the kingdom of Jesus ... on the tree" (8:5). Numbers has a priest and a clean man, not children; the Mishnah tractate Parah has children raised in purity who drew the water and, in Rabbi Yose the Galilean's view, sprinkled one another (Mishnah Parah 3:2-4).

sections.h: The Epistle of Barnabas: food laws as moral lessons
sections.b: For Barnabas, "God's commandment is not about not eating" (Barnabas 10:2). Moses forbade the pig because some people remember God only when hungry, birds of prey because some rob instead of working, scaleless fish of the deep because some are hopelessly ungodly (10:3-5); the hare, the hyena and the weasel stand for sexual sins (10:6-8). Clean animals that chew the cud and split the hoof stand for those who meditate on the word and walk in this world while waiting for the next (10:11), a reading Philo had given (On the Special Laws 4.106-108). Unlike Philo, and unlike the New Testament, which says the food laws were set aside in Christ (Mark 7:19; Acts 10:15), Barnabas says they were never meant as food rules at all.

sections.h: The Epistle of Barnabas: "an evil angel"
sections.b: Barnabas holds that God "circumcised our heart" and our ears (Barnabas 9:1-3) and that circumcision in the flesh was never meant: Israel practiced it "because an evil angel was tricking them" (9:4). He adds that Syrians, Arabs, Egyptians and the priests of idols circumcise too (9:6). Lake sums up this view: "The literal exegesis of the ceremonial law is to him a device of an evil angel who deceived the Jews." It conflicts with Genesis 17:9-14, where God commands it, and with Paul, who opposed circumcising Gentile believers but called circumcision a seal God gave Abraham (Romans 4:11) and of "much" value to the Jew (Romans 3:1-2).
sections.refs: Barnabas 9:1-9; Genesis 17:9-14; Jeremiah 9:25-26; Romans 2:28-29; Romans 3:1-2; Romans 4:11

sections.h: The Epistle of Barnabas: the eighth day
sections.b: Barnabas 15 argues that no one can keep the Sabbath holy now, since it must be kept "with clean hands and a clean heart" (Barnabas 15:1, 15:6), and that God's true rest comes after six thousand years (15:4-5). God says he does not accept "the Sabbaths of the present time" but will make "the beginning of an eighth day, which is the beginning of another world." "That is why we also keep the eighth day with gladness. It is the day on which Jesus rose from the dead" (15:8-9). It is an early witness that Christians kept Sunday and gave it a meaning of its own.
sections.refs: Barnabas 15:1-9; Exodus 20:8-11; Isaiah 1:13; Acts 20:7; Revelation 1:10; Didache 14:1

sections.h: The Epistle of Barnabas: the building and the heart
sections.b: Barnabas says Israel hoped in the building and made God holy in the temple "almost the way the nations do" (Barnabas 16:1-2), quoting Isaiah 40:12 and 66:1 as Stephen does in Acts 7:49. "Those who tore this temple down will build it themselves" (16:3), and "now the very servants of their enemies will build it up again" (16:4), a line Lake says "is supposed to refer to the events of 132 A.D.," when Hadrian built a temple to Jupiter on the site (Cassius Dio, Roman History 69.12). The true temple is the believer's heart, once "a house of demons," now built in the name of the Lord (16:6-10).

sections.h: The Epistle of Barnabas: "Yes, it is ours"
sections.b: Barnabas calls it a sin to say "The covenant is theirs and ours" (Barnabas 4:6). Israel, he says, lost it at Sinai when Moses broke the tablets (4:7-8; 14:1-3); "they were not worthy to receive it" (14:1), and the Lord himself gave it to us (14:4-5). This conflicts with the Old Testament, where God renews the covenant after the golden calf (Exodus 34:1-10), and with Paul, for whom the covenants belong to Israel (Romans 9:4) and God's call is not taken back (Romans 11:29). The Catholic Church's Nostra Aetate 4 says that "the Jews should not be presented as rejected or accursed by God."
sections.refs: Barnabas 4:6-8; Barnabas 13:1; Barnabas 14:1-5; Exodus 34:1-10; Romans 9:4; Romans 11:29

sections.h: The Epistle of Barnabas: sealed in the heart
sections.b: For Barnabas the stone tablets were smashed "so that the covenant of Jesus the Beloved might be sealed into our hearts" (Barnabas 4:8), and the Lord came to "set up the covenant in us" by his word (14:5). He applies Ezekiel's promise of hearts of flesh for hearts of stone to believers (6:14). Jeremiah's new covenant is made "with the house of Israel" (Jeremiah 31:31); Barnabas sets it against Israel.
sections.refs: Barnabas 4:8; Barnabas 6:14; Barnabas 14:5-7; Jeremiah 31:31-34; Ezekiel 36:26; 2 Corinthians 3:3

sections.h: The Epistle of Barnabas
sections.b: The Epistle of Barnabas is among the sharpest early Christian writings about Jews and Judaism. It says Israel lost the covenant at Sinai (Barnabas 4:7-8; 14:1-4), that circumcision in the flesh came from an evil angel's deception (9:4), that the food laws were never meant to be kept (10:2, 10:9), that the Temple was a pagan error (16:1-2), and that Christ came so that those who killed the prophets would fill up their sins (5:11; 14:5). Lake describes its aim as warning Christians "against a Judaistic conception of the Old Testament." Its charges conflict with Paul (Romans 9:4-5; 11:1-2, 28-29). The Catholic Church's Nostra Aetate 4 says that God "holds the Jews most dear for the sake of their Fathers" and that "the Jews should not be presented as rejected or accursed by God."
sections.refs: Barnabas 4:6-8; Barnabas 5:11; Barnabas 9:4; Barnabas 14:1-5; Barnabas 16:1-2; Romans 9:4-5; Romans 11:1-2; Romans 11:28-29

sections.h: The Epistle of Barnabas: one people only
sections.b: Barnabas asks "whether this people is the heir, or the first one" (Barnabas 13:1) and answers from Genesis: "the greater will serve the lesser" (13:2), Jacob's crossed hands (13:5), and Abraham, "the father of the nations who believe in God while uncircumcised" (13:7). It calls the church "the new people" (5:7; 7:5) and warns against those who say "The covenant is theirs and ours" (4:6). Paul uses the same stories (Romans 9:10-13; 4:9-17) but ends with Israel still beloved and "all Israel will be saved" (Romans 11:26-29). Barnabas has no such ending. It is the clearest early example of the view that the church simply replaces Israel; see the cards on this page.
sections.refs: Barnabas 4:6-8; Barnabas 5:7; Barnabas 13:1-7; Romans 9:10-13; Romans 4:9-17; Romans 11:26-29

sections.h: The Epistle of Barnabas: the law never meant literally
sections.b: Barnabas speaks of "the new law of our Lord Jesus Christ, which has no yoke of force" (Barnabas 2:6), and reads the sacrifices, fasts, food laws, circumcision and Sabbath as lessons that were never meant to be kept to the letter (2-16). Moses "spoke in the Spirit" (10:2, 10:9). Yet the letter ends by urging readers to "learn the Lord's decrees, all that are written, and to walk in them" (21:1). The law for Barnabas is good and holy, if read his way; his quarrel is with those who keep it literally.
sections.refs: Barnabas 2:6; Barnabas 10:2; Barnabas 10:9; Barnabas 21:1; Romans 7:12; Matthew 5:17

sections.h: The Epistle of Barnabas: water and the cross
sections.b: Barnabas 11 looks for baptism in the prophets: Israel would refuse "the baptism that brings forgiveness of sins" (Barnabas 11:1); Psalm 1's tree by the water joins the cross and baptism: "Happy are those who put their hope in the cross and went down into the water" (11:8); and "we go down into the water loaded with sins and filth, and come up bearing fruit in the heart" (11:11). It is an early witness to baptism by going down into water, for forgiveness of sins.

sections.h: The Epistle of Barnabas: the tree
sections.b: Barnabas finds the cross everywhere: "he had to suffer on a tree" (Barnabas 5:13); the wool on wood means "the kingdom of Jesus is on the tree" (8:5); in Greek numbers the 300 of Genesis 14:14 is T, the shape of the cross (9:8); Psalm 1's tree by the water joins cross and baptism (11:8); a tree that bends and rises and drips blood (12:1, close to 4 Ezra 5:5); Moses' outstretched arms (12:2) and the bronze snake on wood (12:7).
sections.refs: Barnabas 5:13; Barnabas 8:5; Barnabas 9:8; Barnabas 11:8; Barnabas 12:1-7; Galatians 3:13; 1 Peter 2:24

sections.h: The Epistle of Barnabas: Moses spoke in the Spirit
sections.b: Barnabas calls Moses "the other prophet" (Barnabas 6:8) and says he "spoke in the Spirit" when he gave the food laws (10:2, 10:9). He tells twice how Moses broke the tablets (4:7-8; 14:2-3). Moses' arms raised in battle and the bronze snake are figures of the cross (12:2-7), and Moses gave Joshua the name Jesus (12:8-9). Moses received the covenant "as an attendant"; the Lord gave it to us (14:4), as Hebrews 3:5-6 contrasts Moses and the Son.
sections.refs: Barnabas 4:7-8; Barnabas 6:8; Barnabas 10:2; Barnabas 12:2-9; Barnabas 14:2-4; Hebrews 3:5-6

sections.h: The Epistle of Barnabas: father of believers, and the 318
sections.b: Barnabas uses Abraham twice. He is the one who "first gave circumcision" and looked ahead to Jesus: his 318 men spell Jesus and the cross (Barnabas 9:7-8). And he is the one God made "the father of the nations who believe in God while uncircumcised" (13:7), Paul's point in Romans 4:11 put into God's mouth. The three children who sprinkle the heifer's water stand for Abraham, Isaac and Jacob (8:4).
sections.refs: Barnabas 8:4; Barnabas 9:7-8; Barnabas 13:7; Genesis 14:14; Genesis 15:6; Genesis 17:5; Romans 4:9-17

sections.h: The Epistle of Barnabas: the younger chosen
sections.b: Barnabas reads Rebekah's twins as two peoples, with "the greater" serving "the lesser" (Barnabas 13:2-3), and Jacob's crossed hands over Ephraim and Manasseh as "a figure of the people to come" (13:5). Jacob in Barnabas speaks the words of Genesis 25:23 to Joseph. The "lesser" is the church, the "greater" Israel.

sections.h: The Epistle of Barnabas: Ephraim and Manasseh
sections.b: In Barnabas 13:4-6 Joseph brings his sons to Jacob and asks him to move his right hand to Manasseh, the firstborn; Jacob says, "I know, my child, I know. But the greater will serve the lesser." Barnabas reads the younger Ephraim as the church.

sections.h: The Epistle of Barnabas: the ten kings
sections.b: Barnabas quotes Daniel 7:24 and 7:7-8 freely: ten kingdoms, a small king rising after them who brings down three, the fourth beast and its little horn (Barnabas 4:4-5). He applies it to his own time, the "complete stumbling block" (4:3). Lake reports that some have counted ten Roman emperors here to date the letter in the first century, "though there is no unanimity as to the exact manner in which the number of the ten Emperors is to be reached."

sections.h: The Epistle of Barnabas
sections.b: Barnabas names Daniel and quotes Daniel 7 in a form that matches neither Greek version exactly (Barnabas 4:4-5). In 16:6 Lake's margin compares Daniel's seventy weeks with Barnabas's saying that the temple will be built "when the week is completed."

sections.h: The Epistle of Barnabas: the Servant who suffers
sections.b: Barnabas quotes the Servant songs of Isaiah for Christ's passion and mission: Isaiah 53:5, 7 (Barnabas 5:2), Isaiah 50:6-9 (5:14-6:2, where Barnabas speaks of "the Lord's servant"), Isaiah 42:6-7 and 49:6 (14:7-8), and Isaiah 61:1-2 (14:9). He reads them as the Father's words to the Son.
sections.refs: Barnabas 5:2; Barnabas 5:14; Barnabas 6:1-2; Barnabas 14:7-9; Isaiah 42:6-7; Isaiah 49:6; Isaiah 50:6-9; Isaiah 53:5-7; Isaiah 61:1-2

sections.h: The Epistle of Barnabas: a second creation
sections.b: "In the last times he made a second creation. And the Lord says: 'Look, I make the last things like the first'" (Barnabas 6:13). Forgiveness makes believers new, with the souls of children, as though God were forming them over again (6:11); Genesis 1:26-28 is spoken of "us" (6:12). In the temple chapter, believers "became new, created all over again from the beginning" (16:8), and at the end God will make all things new and begin "another world" (15:7-8).

sections.h: The Epistle of Barnabas
sections.b: The way of light in Barnabas has the same words as Didache 2:2: "You must not murder a child by abortion, and you must not kill one that has been born either" (Barnabas 19:5). The way of darkness lists "murderers of children and destroyers of what God has formed" (20:2).

sections.h: The Epistle of Barnabas: angels over the two ways
sections.b: "Over the one are stationed light-bringing angels of God, and over the other, angels of Satan" (Barnabas 18:1). Barnabas also blames literal circumcision on "an evil angel" (9:4). Paul and Stephen say the law was given through angels (Galatians 3:19; Acts 7:53) but never call them evil.

sections.h: The Epistle of Barnabas: the Black One
sections.b: Barnabas calls the devil "the one who is at work" (Barnabas 2:1), "the evil one" (2:10; 21:3), "the evil ruler" (4:13), "the ruler of the present time of lawlessness" (18:2), and "the Black One" (4:9; 20:1), a name that goes with the letter's light and darkness, not with skin. The way of darkness is his way (20:1).
sections.refs: Barnabas 2:1; Barnabas 2:10; Barnabas 4:9; Barnabas 4:13; Barnabas 18:1-2; Barnabas 20:1; Barnabas 21:3; John 12:31

sections.h: The Epistle of Barnabas quotes "Enoch"
sections.b: Barnabas cites Enoch twice with formulas for Scripture: "it is written, as Enoch says" (Barnabas 4:3), with no matching passage, and "the Scripture says" before words close to 1 Enoch 89:56 and 89:66, the Lord handing over the sheep, their fold and their tower to destruction (16:5). Lake's margin points to 1 Enoch 89 at both places.

sections.h: The Epistle of Barnabas cites books outside the 66
sections.b: Barnabas treats some writings outside the 66 as Scripture. It cites "Enoch" (Barnabas 4:3) and quotes words close to 1 Enoch 89 as "the Scripture" (16:5). Its prophecy of a tree that bends and rises and drips blood (12:1) is close to 4 Ezra 5:5. Several of its quotations, such as "Look, I make the last things like the first" (6:13), come from no known book.
sections.refs: Barnabas 4:3; Barnabas 6:13; Barnabas 12:1; Barnabas 16:5; 1 Enoch 89:56; 4 Ezra 5:5

sections.h: The Epistle of Barnabas: a Gospel saying "as it is written"
sections.b: Barnabas brings in "The called are many, but the chosen are few" (Matthew 22:14) with "as it is written" (Barnabas 4:14), the formula for Scripture, which may show a Gospel already read as Scripture. The letter itself was quoted as Scripture by Clement of Alexandria and stands in Codex Sinaiticus right after Revelation, Lake says.

sections.h: The Epistle of Barnabas
sections.b: Barnabas gives words in Jesus' voice that no Gospel has: "those who want to see me and lay hold of my kingdom must receive me through hardship and suffering" (Barnabas 7:11). The closest Bible verse is Acts 14:22.

sections.h: The Epistle of Barnabas: the text
sections.b: Barnabas survives in Codex Sinaiticus (300s AD), the Codex Constantinopolitanus (AD 1056), eight later Greek manuscripts that run Polycarp to the Philippians 9 straight into Barnabas 5, and a Latin version that ends at 17:2, as Lake lists them. So chapters 1-4 rest on Sinaiticus, C and the Latin only, and 18-21 on the Greek alone. Lake's 36 footnotes record where they differ.
